new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (51 pp., I.R.I.S. scan, no text layer; extracted text on p. 2 returns only a form feed). Rendered PDF page 2 (printed p. ii, 'Introduction') at 150 dpi and read the image directly: the passage sits immediately under the ruled phoneme table and reads exactly 'Stress is generally on the penultimate vowel, or on the last vowel followed by a consonant. Words with final stress are written with two vowels at the end of the word.' -- verbatim match to the reported quote and to the scanned file we hold. The page also carries the phoneme table (pw p t k kw; bw b d ŋg; mw m n ŋ; v[β] z g[g]~[ɣ]; s; l r; w y; i e a o u), exactly as the report describes. Reading: default penult, with a final clo…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the penultimate vowel unless the word ends in a consonant, in which case the final (closed) syllable is stressed; final stress on a vowel-final word is represented in the orthography by writing the final vowel double (i.e. a final long vowel/VV takes the stress). So: closed or long final syllable attracts stress, otherwise penultimate.
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged with 'generally'; vowel-final words with final stress exist and are spelled with a doubled final vowel; no other exceptions listed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement in the front matter of a vocabulary (citation forms); phonemes listed on the same page (voiceless stops pw p t k kw; prenasalized bw b d ŋg; nasals mw m n ŋ; fricatives v[β] z g[g]~[ɣ], s; l r; w y; vowels i e a o u). Stress is not marked on the entries themselves.
new_statements.identity_note: Lincoln 1977 describes the speech of Gitua Village (shown as Kelanoa on maps, c. 6°S 147°35'E), i.e. the language gitu1237 itself (alt. names Gitoa, Kelana); no dialect split is mentioned. Lincoln's phoneme table shows labiovelars pw bw mw and kw; Ross 1988 and Chowning 1986 confirm the same variety via Lincoln's data.
